page.title: Water and ecosystems
page.description: Invasive species in the Glenabo-Corrin catchment, why they matter, and what one person can do.

hero.title:
Invasive species,
and why they matter here.
hero.intro: An invasive species is one that arrived from elsewhere and spreads without the checks that held it in balance at home.

items.alt: Dense glossy dark green evergreen leaves of cherry laurel
items.title: Cherry laurel
items.text: Evergreen, dense, and casts shade so deep that nothing grows beneath it. Spreads readily from garden plantings into woodland.

items.alt: A truss of pale lilac rhododendron flowers above dark leathery leaves
items.title: Rhododendron
items.text: Forms impenetrable thickets, prevents woodland regenerating, and is difficult and expensive to remove once established.

items.alt: Broad shovel-shaped knotweed leaves on red-flecked stems, backlit
items.title: Japanese knotweed
items.text: Spreads from small fragments of root or stem. Cutting or moving soil makes it worse. Report it - do not attempt to clear it yourself.

items.alt: A grey squirrel crouched along a branch, tail curved over its back
items.title: Grey squirrel
items.text: Displaces the native red squirrel and strips bark from young broadleaf trees.

items.alt: A dark brown mink standing side-on, low body and long tail
items.title: American mink
items.text: Predates ground-nesting birds and fish along watercourses.

items.alt: An Asian hornet feeding on a white umbel, dark thorax and orange-banded abdomen
items.title: Asian hornet
items.text: A serious threat to honeybees and other pollinators. Any suspected sighting should be reported immediately.

items.heading: Check your own garden
items.text: Laurel and rhododendron spread into woodland from garden plantings.

items.heading: Clean your boots between sites
items.text: Seeds and fragments travel in mud. A brush down at the car park is enough.

items.heading: Record what you see
items.text: Records build the picture of what lives here.

items.heading: Do not cut or move Japanese knotweed
items.text: It spreads from fragments of root and stem, so cutting it or shifting the soil around it moves it rather than removes it. Report it and leave it where it is.

items.heading: Do not dump garden waste in woodland
items.text: Garden plants arrive in woodland this way. Cuttings, roots and seed heads tipped over a wall or at the end of a track can establish where they land.

items.heading: Do not move soil between sites
items.text: Seeds and fragments travel in soil as readily as in mud on a boot. Soil brought in from elsewhere brings whatever was living in it.
